summary:
Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex sexual activity, dating from the French protectorate period through independence in 1953, and gender expression is not criminalised. The statutory framework nonetheless contains no SOGI non-discrimination provisions, and no legal gender recognition procedure is in force.

The state's posture toward sexual orientation and gender identity is formally cooperative. At its 2019 Universal Periodic Review Cambodia accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage, and at the 2024 review it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations, covering marriage equality, legal gender recognition based on self-defined identity, and anti-discrimination measures. Acceptance is a stated commitment; the inventory contains no evidence that implementing legislation has been enacted. Cambodia also hosted the visit of the UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, whose report identifies good practices, remaining challenges and recommendations to strengthen protection against violence and discrimination, and was circulated to national stakeholders in an unofficial Khmer translation.

The operative risks are street-level and detention-level rather than statutory. A Cambodian Centre for Human Rights study documents more than 135 cases of harassment and abuse against transgender women on city streets, describing the treatment as shocking, and records a police practice in Siem Reap in which transgender sex workers were targeted and forced to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water. Comparable abuse is reported across urban centres, including extortion attributed to police.

Violence also originates inside the household. A Rainbow Community Kampuchea study reported in 2019 found that 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 had suffered emotional abuse from a family member, and that 35% of participants in that age group had considered suicide as a result of family rejection; one case involved a 27-year-old trans man sent by his mother to a rehabilitation facility to correct his gender.

Placement in detention is decided case by case rather than by published rule. In February 2025 the president of the Cambodian Human Rights Committee, Keo Remy, stated at a ceremony at Correctional Centre 2 in Prey Sar prison, Phnom Penh, that transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from the men's facility, Correctional Centre 1, to the women's facility, Correctional Centre 2. The remarks praised the centre and cited no statute or formal policy text. The same report notes that prison overcrowding has worsened amid arrests from a gang crackdown.

Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, the two principal cities, have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors, and international guidebooks carry dedicated sections for LGBT travellers. That infrastructure sits alongside the documented street and policing risks rather than displacing them.
tangentialFactors:
Cambodia's non-criminalisation is long-standing rather than recent: same-sex activity was never prohibited under the French protectorate administration or after independence in 1953, which distinguishes it from neighbouring jurisdictions that retained or introduced such offences.

The trajectory of official engagement runs through the Universal Periodic Review process, with marriage-equality recommendations accepted in 2019 and a full set of 12 SOGIESC recommendations accepted in 2024, alongside the visit of the UN Independent Expert. The gap between accepted recommendations and enacted law is the central unresolved question for anyone assessing legal certainty on arrival.

The documented evidence base is uneven in age. The UNDP and USAID country report, Being LGBT in Asia: Cambodia, dates from 2014 and rests on a national LGBT community dialogue held in Phnom Penh in January 2013, participant interviews, an NGO and CBO survey and a literature review; it describes the legal and social environment as it stood a decade ago and should not be read as current law.

Family-level rejection is a documented driver of harm for younger Cambodians, with the RoCK findings concentrated on people under 35, which points to a risk profile that differs between visitors, who are largely outside family structures, and residents.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition based on self-defined identity was accepted as a recommendation at the 2024 Universal Periodic Review but no implementing statute is recorded, so residents still have no established route to amend gender markers on official documents.

Legislation contains no SOGI non-discrimination provisions, leaving employment, housing, health and education complaints without a statutory basis, despite anti-discrimination measures being among the accepted 2024 recommendations.

Family violence against queer and transgender young people is widespread in the available data: 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 reported emotional abuse by a family member, and 35% of that group had considered suicide because of family rejection.

Transgender prisoners who have undergone sex-change surgery are moved from Correctional Centre 1 to Correctional Centre 2 at Prey Sar, according to Keo Remy of the Cambodian Human Rights Committee in February 2025. The transfer practice was announced publicly rather than published as regulation, so it offers no enforceable entitlement, and it is unclear how it applies to detainees who have not had surgery.

Civil-society organisations including Rainbow Community Kampuchea and the Cambodian Centre for Human Rights produce the substantive documentation on LGBT conditions, and submitted jointly to the 4th-cycle Universal Periodic Review in December 2023.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 12 Universal Periodic Review recommendations accepted in 2024, including the seven on marriage equality, have been translated into legislation is unresolved in this inventory; no implementing bill, statute or court judgment is cited.

The prison transfer practice described in February 2025 rests on a ministerial-level statement at an event, not on a published regulation. No statute or formal policy text is available to confirm its scope, its criteria or whether it binds the prison administration.

Hate-crime law, entry and visa rules for transgender travellers, document screening at ports of entry, and access to gender-affirming healthcare are not addressed by any source in this inventory and remain unsourced here.

The CCHR figures on street harassment and the Siem Reap policing practice are reported through press coverage of the study; the underlying report's methodology, sample and time period are not reproduced in the sources available for this pass.

The UN Independent Expert visit report is referenced through the UN Cambodia page, which summarises its scope; the recommendations themselves were not available for review in this pass.
